q: Acrytex acrylic paint is made by which company?
n: Acrytex is Boysen's line of acrylic paints and primers. Boysen is made by Pacific Paint (Boysen) Philippines, Inc. Source: Boysen company website.

q: Which durable, flexible paint is used on exterior walls and applied in very thick films?
n: Elastomeric paint is applied in very thick films that stay flexible, stretch over hairline cracks and shed rain, which suits exterior walls. Source: ASTM D6904 (resistance to wind-driven rain); paint manufacturer data (Boysen, Davies).

q: Which glossy, quick-drying solvent paint with resin is mainly used on furniture?
n: Lacquer is a glossy, fast-drying coating of resin (nitrocellulose or acrylic) dissolved in solvent. It dries by evaporation in minutes and is the classic furniture finish. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (finishes).

q: Which paint cannot be thinned with water?
n: Enamel (alkyd or oil-based) is solvent-borne and is thinned with paint thinner or mineral spirits, not water. Acrylic, latex and emulsion paints are water-borne. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature (Boysen, Davies).

q: Why is concrete neutralizer applied before painting new walls?
o: To counter the alkalinity of new concrete
To keep the concrete from burning the paint
n: New concrete and plaster contain free lime and are strongly alkaline. A neutralizer reduces this alkalinity so it does not attack (saponify) the paint binder and cause peeling or discoloration. Source: Boysen technical literature (masonry neutralizer); ASTM D4262 (pH of concrete).

q: What paint suits rooms that need frequent cleaning, like kitchens and baths?
n: Enamel dries to a hard, non-porous, washable film that resists grease and moisture, so it suits kitchens, toilets and areas that are cleaned often. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature.

q: What paint is usually specified for interior ceilings?
n: Interior ceilings are usually specified with flat or matte acrylic (water-based) paint, which hides surface flaws, reduces glare and dries fast. Source: Paint manufacturer specification guides (Boysen, Davies).

q: What paint is specified for baseboards and trim?
n: Baseboards and trim are knocked and wiped often, so they are finished with hard, glossy enamel. Source: Paint manufacturer specification guides.

q: What paint is specified for interior walls?
n: Interior walls are typically finished with latex (water-based emulsion) paint: low odor, quick-drying, washable and easy to recoat. Source: Paint manufacturer specification guides.

q: Which durable paint is specified for exterior walls?
n: 100% acrylic exterior paint resists UV, rain, alkali and chalking far better than alkyds, so it is the standard durable exterior wall paint. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature; ASTM D4141 (weathering).

q: Which defect shows as small to medium bubbles under the film, common on wood siding and trim?
n: Blistering is the formation of bubbles under the paint film, caused by moisture or solvent vapor pushing the film up, typically on wood siding and trim in sun. Source: Paint defect guides (Sherwin-Williams, Boysen); US Forest Service Wood Handbook.

q: Which defect is a deep-relief crack pattern like reptile skin?
n: Alligatoring is a pattern of deep, wide cracks resembling reptile skin, caused by hard coats over soft ones or by aging of oil films. Source: Paint defect guides; US Forest Service Wood Handbook.

q: Which defect is like alligatoring but milder, with long, evenly spaced, shallow cracks?
n: Checking is a milder form of cracking: shallow, short cracks in the top coat that do not reach the substrate. Source: Paint defect guides; US Forest Service Wood Handbook.

q: Which defect shows crusty white salt deposits pushing through paint on masonry?
n: Efflorescence is white crystalline salt carried out of masonry or concrete by moisture and deposited on or through the paint surface. Source: ASTM C67 (efflorescence test); paint defect guides.

q: Which defect is a fine powder forming on the paint surface?
n: Chalking is a fine powder on the paint surface. UV and weathering break down the binder and release pigment particles. Source: ASTM D4214 (degree of chalking).

q: Which defect shows as drips or drooping in the film?
n: Sagging is drips, curtains or drooping of the wet film, caused by applying too heavy a coat or over-thinned paint. Source: Paint defect guides; ASTM D4400 (sag resistance).

q: Which defect is a fungus growing on paint or caulk, seen as gray, brown, green or black spots?
n: Mildew is a fungus that grows on paint and caulk in damp, shaded areas, showing as gray, brown, green or black spots. Source: ASTM D3274 (fungal growth on paint); paint defect guides.

q: Which defect shows reddish-brown to black stains on the paint?
n: Rust discoloration is reddish-brown to black staining where corroding nails, bars or metal bleed through the coating. Source: Paint defect guides; SSPC surface preparation standards.

q: Paint separating from an earlier coat or the substrate, leaving some paint behind, signals:
o: Peeling from moisture behind the film
n: When paint separates from an earlier coat or the substrate and leaves some paint behind, the bond itself has failed: poor adhesion from dirty, glossy or chalky surfaces. Source: Paint defect guides; ASTM D3359 (adhesion by tape test).

q: Cracking and gradual peeling of paint caused by moisture getting behind the film signals:
o: Peeling from moisture behind the film
n: Moisture getting behind the film (from leaks, condensation or rising damp) breaks the bond, causing cracking and progressive peeling down to the substrate. Source: Paint defect guides; US Forest Service Wood Handbook.

q: Paint containing a considerable amount of varnish is generally called:
n: Enamel is essentially pigmented varnish: paint with a large proportion of varnish (resin) binder, so it dries hard and glossy. Source: Paint technology references; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which additive makes dirt easier to clean off paint?
n: PTFE (Teflon) additives lower the surface energy of the film, so dirt and stains do not stick and can be wiped off easily. Source: Paint manufacturer literature on PTFE-modified coatings.

q: In paint, VOC stands for:
n: VOC means volatile organic compound: solvents that evaporate as paint dries and contribute to indoor pollution and smog. Low-VOC paints are favored in green building. Source: US EPA, Volatile Organic Compounds' Impact on Indoor Air Quality; Philippine Green Building Code.

q: What thins latex paint?
n: Latex paint is water-borne, so it is thinned and cleaned up with water. Lacquer thinner and turpentine are for solvent-borne coatings. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature.

q: What type of paint is applied before the finishing coat?
n: A primer is applied to the bare surface before the finish coats. It seals porosity, gives adhesion and, on metal, inhibits rust. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature; SSPC paint system guides.

q: What household material can be used to remove fungus on paint that causes the wall to turn pink?
n: Pink staining on damp paint is fungal or bacterial growth. Washing with a disinfectant (bleach solution) kills it before repainting with a mildew-resistant paint. Source: US EPA, Mold Cleanup guidance; paint manufacturer maintenance guides.

q: What type of paint should be used to resist molds, fungus, and mildew?
n: Polyurethane coatings form a hard, non-porous, highly washable film with good moisture resistance, so mold and mildew have little to grow on. Source: Paint manufacturer technical literature.

q: What is a common sign of mold or mildew on paint?
n: Mold and mildew show as discolored patches or spots (gray, green, black or pink), unlike the white powder of chalking or the bubbles of blistering. Source: ASTM D3274; US EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold.

q: What mainly causes mold and mildew on interior walls?
n: Mold grows where moisture lingers: high humidity, condensation and poor ventilation in toilets, kitchens and closets. Source: US EPA, A Brief Guide to Mold, Moisture and Your Home.

q: Which finish best resists mold in bathrooms?
n: Semi-gloss and gloss films are less porous and shed moisture, and they can be scrubbed, so mold has less to hold onto in bathrooms. Source: Paint manufacturer specification guides; US EPA mold guidance.

q: What is the best primer for metal?
n: Alkyd (oil-based) primers with rust-inhibitive pigments wet out and bond to steel and slow corrosion, so they are the standard primer for metal. Source: SSPC Paint Specs; paint manufacturer technical literature.

q: What is the best paint for concrete?
n: Acrylic paints resist alkali, so they suit concrete. Oil and alkyd paints saponify (turn soapy and peel) on alkaline masonry. Source: ASTM D4262; paint manufacturer technical literature.

q: Which paint provides a weatherproof coating with a high sheen for exterior walls?
n: Gloss latex gives a weatherproof, high-sheen exterior film that sheds water and dirt. Flat latex has no sheen and quick-drying enamel (QDE) is meant for wood and metal. Source: Paint manufacturer specification guides.

q: Which type of paint contains oil in its formulation?
n: Oil-based paint uses drying oils (such as linseed) or oil-modified binders. That oil content is what defines it, as against water-borne emulsions. Source: Paint technology references.

q: Which paint finish is best used for interior walls?
n: Semi-gloss is often specified for interior walls that need washability and moisture resistance, such as halls, kitchens and toilets, while still keeping a soft sheen. Source: Paint manufacturer specification guides.

q: One gallon covers 25 m² for the first coat. How many gallons are needed for both faces of a 10 m × 30 m wall?
n: Both faces = 2 × (10 × 30) = 600 m². At 25 m² per gallon, 600 ÷ 25 = 24 gallons. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (painting).

q: A 5 m × 5 m room has a 2.4 m ceiling, two 1.0 × 1.2 m windows and a 2.0 × 1.0 m door. If 4 L (one gallon) covers 25 m², how many gallons are needed for one coat on the walls?
n: Walls = 4 × 5.0 × 2.4 = 48 m², less openings (2 × 1.2 + 2.0 = 4.4 m²) = 43.6 m². At 25 m² per gallon, 43.6 ÷ 25 = 1.74, so buy 2 gallons. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (painting).

q: One pail of paint is how many gallons?
n: Locally, paint is sold in liters, quarts (1 L), gallons (about 4 L) and pails of 4 gallons (about 16 L). Source: Paint manufacturer packaging (Boysen, Davies); Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: How many liters does a local "gallon" of paint hold?
n: Philippine paint "gallons" are 4-liter cans (close to the US gallon of 3.785 L). Source: Paint manufacturer packaging (Boysen, Davies).

q: How many pints are in one gallon?
n: One US gallon = 4 quarts = 8 pints. A quart is 2 pints, so 4 quarts make 8 pints. An imperial gallon also has 8 (larger) pints. Source: NIST Handbook 44, units of measure.

q: Which brand is best known for removing rust?
n: Turco is a locally known brand of metal treatment and rust-removing products. Davies, Boysen and Nippon are general paint brands. Source: Philippine hardware supplier catalogs.

q: Which company makes Megacryl paint?
n: Megacryl is Davies Paints Philippines' acrylic latex paint line. Source: Davies Paints company website.

q: Which brand makes Liquid Tile?
n: Liquid Tile is Davies' epoxy-type high-gloss coating for walls and floors that gives a tile-like, washable finish. Source: Davies Paints company website.

q: Which brand offers a roof paint product called "Roofgard"?
n: Roofgard is Boysen's water-based gloss acrylic roof paint for galvanized iron. Source: Boysen company website.

q: Weatherbond is a product line of which paint company?
n: Weatherbond is Nippon Paint's premium exterior acrylic wall paint line. Source: Nippon Paint Philippines company website.

q: Which of the following is a passage doorknob, used for interior doors that do not need locking, such as hallway or closet doors?
n: A passage knob (Figure B) has knobs on both sides that only retract the latch, with no lock. It is used for halls and closets. Source: BHMA A156.2 lock functions; lockset manufacturer catalogs.

q: Which of the following is a storeroom doorknob, typically used for doors that always remain locked from the outside and require a key to open?
n: A storeroom knob is always locked on the outside, opening only with a key, while the inside knob is always free. Figure D matches this function. Source: BHMA A156.2 lock functions.

q: Which of the following is a privacy doorknob, designed for bedrooms or bathrooms where locking from the inside is needed?
n: A privacy knob locks from the inside by push-button or turn-button, with an emergency release outside, so it suits bedrooms and bathrooms. Source: BHMA A156.2 lock functions.

q: Which of the following is a keyed doorknob, commonly used for entry doors that require locking and unlocking with a key?
n: A keyed (entry) knob has a key cylinder on the outside and a turn or push-button inside, used for main doors. Figure A shows the key cylinder. Source: BHMA A156.2 lock functions.
